newsitem.title: USA: Economic straits pushed N. Korea into peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Economic straits pushed N. Korea into peace talks.

text.p: Dire economic problems and a lack of friends in the post-communist world pushed North Korea into a breakthrough agreement to start four-party talks on a peace treaty for the Korean peninsula, U.S. officials say.
The isolated and currently famine-stricken Stalinist state gave its formal assent on Monday to the talks proposal at a meeting in New York with U.S. and South Korean officials.
The three countries and China, the fourth party, will meet in New York on Aug. 5 to decide the date, venue, agenda and procedures for the formal start of the peace talks.

For Washington and Seoul, the benefits of a permanent peace in Korea are obvious. The question has always been: what would North Korea gain from a deal that would inevitably mean some degree of accommodation with its hated southern rival?

Ever since U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam jointly proposed the talks in April of last year, U.S. officials have predicted that economic pressures would force Pyongyang to agree sooner or later.
After flooding devastated the country's rice crop in 1995 and 1996, a desperate need for food seems to have clinched North Korea's acceptance.
Until this week, North Korean officials had held out for major food aid on top of the limited quantities it has so far received as a condition for attending the talks.

The United States has so far pledged $25 million and South Korea $16 million in response to the latest appeal by the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) for 203,000 metric tons or $95.5 million of food for North Korea.

U.S. officials insisted on Tuesday that they had not gone beyond a general promise to consider future similar appeals, but the subject is expected to come up at the peace talks and already there are signs more food aid is on the way.

"I'd like for us to do more now and I think you'll see ... other countries willing to do more as well," Clinton said on June 22 at the Group of Seven summit in Denver. The European Union on Tuesday announced the supply of 15,480 metric tons of maize to North Korea.
But U.S. officials said the issue went beyond food to the general question of North Korea's crumbling command economy, in which upward of one quarter of gross national product is spent on defence.
"The existence of the communist bloc was of some benefit to the North Koreans -- other countries would trade with them on a non-market basis," one official said.

"But their economy isn't doing very well. Their system of friendships has been altered by the collapse of communism. If they wish to alter their prospects their best chance is to alter their relationships with their neighbours."

"What's in it for them is a chance to end the state of war that has existed for 47 years and have the opportunity to live in peace and friendship with neighbours and attract trade and investment," the official added.
The proposed peace treaty would replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War, which pitted the Chinese-backed North Koreans against South Korean and U.S.-led U.N. forces.

The North Koreans themselves have been dissatisfied for some time with the armistice arrangements but wanted to talk peace among what they called the "real powers" -- themselves and the United States, excluding South Korea.
Washington insisted this was "not realistic" and that its ally South Korea had to be included. "There can't be peace unless there is peace between the Koreans," one official said.
Still, North Korea has much to hope for from the United States should a peace deal be reached, including diplomatic relations with Washington and an end to U.S. trade sanctions.
For the United States, the stakes are also high. Some 37,000 U.S. troops remain in South Korea, ranged alongside Seoul's forces against a million-strong North Korean army.

U.S. strategy for years has been to seek some kind of soft landing for North Korea that would head off a new Korean war. In 1994, U.S. and North Korean officials struck a deal freezing Pyongyang's nuclear programme in return for supply of new South Korean-made nuclear power generators.
But after more than a year spent setting up the four-party negotiations, no one anticipates that the talks themselves will be either quick or easy.

"I don't think anyone expects that after a few days they will all come out and say there's a peace agreement on the Korean peninsula. There are difficult issues to discuss. It's going to take some effort to overcome these," a U.S. official said.
